title: Living Worthy of God, at Home and in Church
sum: Clement turns from the harmony of creation (chapter 20) to the conduct it calls for. God's many kindnesses can become a judgment if the church does not live "as citizens worthy of him" in harmony (21:1). God sees every thought, like a lamp searching the inner rooms (21:2–3, quoting Proverbs 20:27), so deserting the post he assigned is folly (21:4). Better to offend boastful men than God (21:5).

Then comes a household code: reverence for Christ, whose blood was given for us; respect for leaders; honor for the old; training for the young; and guidance for wives, who are to show purity, gentleness, a restrained tongue and love without favorites (21:6–7). Children are to learn humility, pure love and the fear of God (21:8). God's breath is in us, and he can take it back (21:9).
readings: Read as household instruction
The chapter gives each member of a Christian household a duty, in the order Titus 2 and 1 Peter 2–3 follow. Its picture of the wife is the ideal of its time: modest, gentle, quiet.
Read as a word to a divided church

Every virtue named is the opposite of what Clement sees at Corinth: arrogant talk (21:5), taking sides (21:7), disrespect for leaders and the old (21:6; compare 3:3). The household is a small model of the church at peace.

views.H: The household code is a known form of early Christian teaching (Colossians 3; Ephesians 5–6; 1 Peter 2–3; Titus 2). Clement's version is addressed to men as heads of households and folds church leaders into it ("our leaders").
views.N: Clement's words recall Philippians 1:27 ("live as citizens worthy"), Hebrews 4:12 (God searching "musings"), and 1 Timothy 5:21 (no "leaning to one side"). The order of duties is close to Titus 2 and 1 Peter 5:5.
views.J: The proof text is Proverbs 20:27, in a Greek form unlike both the Hebrew and the Septuagint. "The fear of God" as the goal of training is the language of Proverbs (Proverbs 1:7).
views.G: "Living as citizens" (politeuomai) and "harmony" (homonoia) are political words: Clement speaks of the church as a city whose peace depends on each member keeping his place.

echoes: Proverbs 20:27; Psalm 139:23; Philippians 1:27; Hebrews 4:12; 1 Timothy 5:21; Titus 2:2–5; 1 Peter 3:1–7; Colossians 3:18–21; Genesis 2:7

settings.what: Appeal to live worthily of God, with a household code
settings.by: The church of God in Rome, speaking as one body (tradition names Clement as the writer)
settings.to: The church of God at Corinth, "beloved," where a few members had led a revolt and removed elders who had served well (44:6; 47:6)
settings.when: after the long survey of creation's order (20), as the letter turns to conduct
settings.why: To show that the peace the Corinthians had lost begins at home and in respect for leaders and elders, and that God, who sees every thought, will judge those who stir up strife. Knowing that the audience is a church in revolt makes every household virtue a pointed reminder.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

title: Christ Calls in the Words of Psalm 34
sum: Faith in Christ confirms all this, and Christ himself speaks through the Holy Spirit in Psalm 34: "Come here, children, and hear me out; I will teach you the fear of the Lord" (22:1). The psalm asks who wants life, and answers: guard the tongue, turn from evil, do good, "Look for peace and run after it" (22:2–5). The Lord's eyes are on the righteous and his face against evildoers (22:6). The righteous man cries and is rescued (22:7), and a line from Psalm 32 ends the quotation: mercy surrounds those who hope in the Lord (22:8).

views.N: 1 Peter 3:10–12 quotes the same lines of Psalm 34 to teach Christians to answer insult with blessing. Clement and 1 Peter both use the psalm for the speech that makes peace.
views.J: The quotation follows the Septuagint (Psalm 33:12–18) closely, with Clement's singular "the righteous man" at 22:7 and Psalm 32:10 joined at the end, a Jewish way of linking texts by theme.
views.H: The Syriac version adds Psalm 34:19 after 22:7; Lake judges it an insertion from the Septuagint (see the variant).

settings.what: Psalm 34:11–17 and 32:10, quoted as Christ's own call
settings.by: Christ, speaking through the Holy Spirit in the psalm, as Clement presents it (the psalm itself bears David's name)
settings.to: "Children": in the psalm, those willing to be taught; in the letter, the Corinthian church
settings.why: To put the call to guard the tongue and "run after" peace in the mouth of Christ himself, so that the Corinthians hear their quarrel judged by their Lord.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

title: Do Not Doubt: The Vine Will Ripen
sum: God the Father is merciful and gives gladly to those who come with an undivided mind, so Christians must not be double-minded about his gifts (23:1–2). Clement quotes a "Scripture" no one has found: "Miserable are the double-minded" who say they heard the promises in their fathers' days and have grown old waiting (23:3). The answer is a vine: leaf, bud, flower, sour grape, ripe cluster. In a short time the fruit is ripe (23:4). God's will is coming quickly; the Lord will come suddenly to his temple (23:5, from Isaiah 13:22 and Malachi 3:1 in Greek forms).
readings: Read as a word about the end
The doubters deny that the Lord will come and the dead will rise; Clement answers with the promise of his sudden coming (23:5) and turns to the resurrection (24).
Read as a word about faith in God's gifts
The chapter is framed by God's generosity (23:1) and the soul's fancies about his gifts (23:2). Double-mindedness is any half-trust in what God has promised.

views.H: The quotation of 23:3–4 is found also in 2 Clement 11:2–4, where it is "the prophetic word." Lake: it "cannot be identified"; some think it is from the lost book of Eldad and Modad, which the Shepherd of Hermas cites (Shepherd of Hermas 7:4). Clement's Bible held texts that were later lost.
views.N: The complaint answered here is the one of 2 Peter 3:3–4, and the comfort is that of James 1:5–8 and Hebrews 10:36–37.
views.J: Isaiah 13:22, about Babylon's doom, and Malachi 3:1, about the Lord coming to his temple, are joined and reapplied in Greek forms that differ from the Hebrew; "the Holy One" stands where Malachi has "the messenger of the covenant."

echoes: James 1:5–8; 2 Peter 3:3–10; Matthew 24:32–33; Isaiah 13:22; Malachi 3:1; Hebrews 10:37; 2 Clement 11:2–4

settings.what: Warning against double-mindedness
settings.by: The church of God in Rome, speaking as one body (tradition names Clement as the writer)
settings.to: The church of God at Corinth, "beloved," where a few members had led a revolt and removed elders who had served well (44:6; 47:6)
settings.why: To steady a church in which some had stopped trusting God's promises, and to set up the proofs of the resurrection that follow.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

settings.what: An unidentified "Scripture" on the double-minded
settings.by: An unnamed writing that Clement calls "the Scripture" (Lake: perhaps the lost Book of Eldad and Modad)
settings.to: In the quotation, "fools" who doubt; in the letter, the Corinthians
settings.when: quoted as Scripture; Lake says the source "cannot be identified"
settings.why: To answer the doubt that God's promises are too slow with a picture of growth that is slow but sure.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

title: Day, Night and the Seed
sum: Clement begins three chapters on the resurrection. God has already raised the Lord Jesus Christ as its "firstfruits" (24:1, as 1 Corinthians 15:20). Nature shows the pattern: night "goes to sleep" and day "rises" (24:3), with the very verbs used for death and resurrection. And seed sown "dry and bare" breaks down in the ground, until the Master's providence raises it up and makes one seed into many (24:4–5).

views.N: Clement follows 1 Corinthians 15 closely: firstfruits (15:20–23) and the bare seed that dies and is raised (15:36–38). He writes to the church that first received those words.
views.G: Day and night and the seed are common pictures; Clement adds the philosophers' word for divine care, pronoia, "providence" (24:5).
views.H: Clement's argument from nature is aimed at people who had grown tired of waiting (23:3).

settings.what: Three proofs of the coming resurrection: nature, the phoenix, and Scripture
settings.by: The church of God in Rome, speaking as one body (tradition names Clement as the writer)
settings.to: The church of God at Corinth, "beloved," where a few members had led a revolt and removed elders who had served well (44:6; 47:6)
settings.why: To restore the hope that some at Corinth had let go, and with it the reason to live humbly and in peace: those who will be raised must live now as God's servants.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

title: The Phoenix
sum: Clement's most famous example. In the lands around Arabia, he says, there is a single bird, the phoenix, that lives five hundred years. When it is about to die it builds a tomb of frankincense, myrrh and spices, enters it and dies. A worm born from its rotting flesh grows wings, and the new bird carries the bones of the old one to Heliopolis in Egypt and lays them on the altar of the sun in full daylight. The priests check their records and find that five hundred years have passed (25:1–5).
readings: Read as natural history
Clement tells the story as fact, as many ancient writers did, and builds an argument on it: if God shows a rising even through a bird, he can surely raise his servants (26:1).
Read as a picture

Tertullian used the bird the same way, as a proof of the resurrection (On the Resurrection of the Flesh 13). Read as a picture, Clement's point survives the legend: the world God made is full of signs of new life.

views.G: The story goes back to Herodotus (2.73), who heard it at Heliopolis and did not believe it; Lake also points to Pliny (Natural History 10.2). Clement's version, with the spice tomb and the worm, differs from Herodotus's ball of myrrh.
views.J: The phoenix is in no Hebrew book. Lake notes that Christians found it in the Greek Psalm 92:12, where phoinix also means "palm."
views.H: Clement wrote from Rome. He gives the story in a form of his own, with the Heliopolis priests' records as proof.

deep.h: The phoenix in ancient writers and the church
deep.b:
Herodotus reports what the priests of Heliopolis told him: the phoenix comes from Arabia once in five hundred years, when its parent dies, and carries the parent to the temple of the Sun in a hollow ball of myrrh. He had seen it only in paintings and says the story did not seem believable to him (Herodotus 2.73, Rawlinson's translation). Lake adds Pliny's Natural History 10.2 "etc." as other witnesses, "with variations."

Clement's form has three features of its own: the bird builds a tomb (sēkos) of spices and dies in it; a worm born from its flesh becomes the new bird; and the priests confirm the date from their records. Each detail serves his argument: death, decay, and a new life that can be checked.

Later Christians used the bird the same way. Tertullian makes it a proof of the resurrection of the flesh and reads the Greek Psalm 92:12 as "The righteous shall flourish like the phœnix" (On the Resurrection of the Flesh 13, Peter Holmes's translation in the Ante-Nicene Fathers).

deep.title: Claude's theory: why Clement chose a bird from Egypt
deep.b: Clement is writing to Corinthians who doubted the resurrection or had tired of waiting for it (23:3). A sign from nature that ordinary educated Greeks had read about in Herodotus could reach them where an appeal to Scripture alone might not. The Heliopolis priests' records add a touch of proof that the event recurs on schedule, like the vine and the seasons of 23:4 and 24:2: God's promises keep time. This is my own reading of Clement's choice; the text gives no reason beyond 26:1.

title: God Will Raise Those Who Served Him
sum: If God shows the greatness of his promise even through a bird, is it any wonder that the Creator will raise those who served him in holiness and good faith (26:1)? Scripture says so: "And you will raise me up, and I will give you thanks," and "I lay down and fell asleep; I woke up, for you are with me" (26:2). And Job: "you will raise up this flesh of mine, which has endured all these things" (26:3).

views.J: Each text is given in a Greek form that differs from the Hebrew. The first matches no psalm exactly (Lake points to Psalm 28:7); the second is Psalm 3:5 with "you are with me"; the third is Job 19:26 with "flesh" for "skin."
views.N: Clement's "flesh" stands beside Paul's "spiritual body" (1 Corinthians 15:44); he stresses that the body that endured will be raised.
views.H: The site's Job 19 page notes that from 1 Clement 26:3 on, Christians read Job 19:25–27 as a prophecy of bodily resurrection.

settings.what: Two psalm lines on rising (close to Psalm 28:7 in the Greek, and Psalm 3:5)
settings.by: The psalmist; the site's Psalm 3 is headed "A psalm of David, when he ran away from his son Absalom," and Psalm 28 "Of David"
settings.to: God, in prayer; in the letter, the Corinthians who doubted the resurrection
settings.when: quoted as Scripture ("it says somewhere"); the first line matches no psalm exactly
settings.why: To show that Scripture itself speaks of being raised up after lying down in sleep.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

settings.what: Job's hope (Job 19:26 in the Greek)
settings.by: Job, answering his friends (Job 19:1)
settings.to: His friends, and God; in the letter, the Corinthians
settings.when: in Job's answer to Bildad (Job 18:1; 19:1), in the middle of his suffering
settings.why: Clement uses the Greek form, "you will raise up this flesh of mine," as a proof that the body will rise.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

title: The God Who Cannot Lie
sum: With this hope the soul should be bound to the God who is faithful in his promises (27:1). He commanded people not to lie and will much less lie himself: "nothing is impossible with God except lying" (27:2). So faith should be kindled again (27:3). His word made all things and can overturn them; no one can say to him "What have you done?"; none of his decrees will pass away (27:4–5). Everything is before him, since the heavens and the days and nights tell of him, and their voices are heard everywhere (27:6–7, Psalm 19 in Greek).

views.J: Psalm 19:1–3 is given from the Septuagint. The Hebrew third line can be read as silence (the site's Psalm 19) or, with the King James Version, as a voice heard everywhere; the Greek has the second sense: every voice is heard. The question of 27:5 is in Wisdom of Solomon 12:12, a book Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include.
views.N: "Impossible that God would lie" is Hebrews 6:18; "will never be gone" echoes Matthew 24:35.

echoes: Hebrews 6:18; Titus 1:2; Numbers 23:19; Wisdom of Solomon 12:12; Psalm 19:1–4; Matthew 24:35; Romans 10:18

settings.what: God sees all and cannot be escaped
settings.by: The church of God in Rome, speaking as one body (tradition names Clement as the writer)
settings.to: The church of God at Corinth, "beloved," where a few members had led a revolt and removed elders who had served well (44:6; 47:6)
settings.when: after the proofs of the resurrection
settings.why: To ground the hope of 24–26 in God's truthfulness, and to warn the rebels that no one can hide from or desert the God who sees all.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

settings.what: The heavens tell God's glory (Psalm 19:1–3 in the Greek)
settings.by: David, as the psalm's heading names him ("A psalm of David")
settings.to: Whoever sings the psalm; in the letter, the Corinthians
settings.why: To show that everything is before God, since his works speak everywhere, so that no one can hide from him (28:1).
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

title: No Place to Run
sum: Since God sees and hears everything, Christians should fear him and leave behind filthy cravings, so that his mercy will shelter them on the day of judgment (28:1). There is nowhere to flee from his hand, and no world will take in a deserter (28:2). Psalm 139 says it: in heaven, at the ends of the earth, in the depths, God is there (28:3). So no one can escape the one who holds all things (28:4).

views.J: Clement gives Psalm 139:7–10 loosely, with "the depths" for Sheol; the form matches neither the Hebrew nor the Septuagint exactly.

settings.what: Nowhere to run from God (Psalm 139:7–10, in Clement's form)
settings.by: David, as the psalm's heading names him ("Of David. A psalm")
settings.to: God, in prayer; in the letter, the Corinthians
settings.why: To warn those who might desert God that there is no place out of his reach.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

title: God's Chosen Portion
sum: So let us come to God in holiness, lifting pure hands, loving the forbearing and tender Father who made us his chosen portion (29:1). Deuteronomy 32:8–9 in Greek says the Most High set the nations' borders by the number of God's angels, but his people Jacob became the Lord's portion (29:2). Another text, found in no known book, says the Lord takes a nation for himself like the firstfruits of a threshing floor, and from it will come "the most holy things" (29:3).

views.J: Clement applies to the church what Deuteronomy says of Israel. The Greek "angels of God" in Deuteronomy 32:8 is one of three readings (see the site's Deuteronomy 32:8 variant). The text of 29:3 cannot be identified; Lake lists verses it resembles and suggests a lost source.
views.N: The church as God's own people echoes 1 Peter 2:9; the raised hands echo 1 Timothy 2:8.
views.O: Clement does not say the church has replaced Israel. He reads Israel's election as now including the Gentile believers of Rome and Corinth; how the churches relate the church and Israel is the card at Galatians 6 and Acts 28.

deep.b: Clement's Greek of Deuteronomy 32:8 says God set the nations' borders "to match the number of the angels of God." The Masoretic Text reads "the sons of Israel"; a Dead Sea Scroll reads "the sons of God," which the site's Deuteronomy follows (see its variant). Read with "angels" or "sons of God," the verse pictures the nations given into the care of heavenly beings while the Lord keeps one people as his own share (Deuteronomy 32:9). Clement does not explore the angels; his point is the second line. God chose "us," as he chose Jacob, and a chosen people must be holy (30:1).

echoes: Deuteronomy 32:8–9; Deuteronomy 4:34; Deuteronomy 14:2; Numbers 18:27; 1 Timothy 2:8; 1 Peter 2:9

settings.what: The chosen portion called to holiness and humility
settings.by: The church of God in Rome, speaking as one body (tradition names Clement as the writer)
settings.to: The church of God at Corinth, "beloved," where a few members had led a revolt and removed elders who had served well (44:6; 47:6)
settings.why: To remind the Corinthians that God chose them as his own, and that such a people must flee slander, uprisings and pride and be justified by works, not words.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

settings.what: The Song of Moses on the nations and the Lord's portion (Deuteronomy 32:8–9 in the Greek)
settings.by: Moses, speaking the song "in the hearing of the whole assembly of Israel" (Deuteronomy 31:30)
settings.to: Israel; in the letter, the church as God's chosen portion
settings.when: the song Moses spoke before the whole assembly (Deuteronomy 31:30)
settings.why: To show that God chose a people for himself out of all the nations, as he has now chosen the church.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

settings.what: An unidentified Scripture on the nation God takes for himself
settings.by: An unnamed writing that Clement introduces with "in another place it says"
settings.to: In the letter, the Corinthians
settings.when: Lake: verses of Deuteronomy, Numbers, 2 Chronicles and Ezekiel "most nearly resemble" it, and "Clement may be referring to some lost source"
settings.why: To show that the chosen people are God's firstfruits and his most holy portion, and so must live in holiness (30:1).
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

title: Holiness, Humility and Few Words
sum: Since we are the Holy One's portion, we must flee slander, impurity, drunkenness, uprisings, adultery and pride (30:1), for God "takes his stand against the proud" and gives grace to the humble (30:2). Join those who have grace; put on harmony; keep away from gossip; be "justified by works, not by words" (30:3). Job 11 in Greek warns against much talk (30:4–5). Praise should come from God, and testimony from others, as it did for the righteous fathers (30:6–7). Boldness and self-will belong to the cursed; forbearance, humility and gentleness to the blessed (30:8).

views.N: Proverbs 3:34 is quoted in the same form as James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5. "Justified by works" sounds like James 2:24, and two chapters later Clement says "through faith" like Romans 3:28: see chapter 32.
views.J: Job 11:2–3 is quoted from the Septuagint, including a line Lake judges corrupt in the Greek itself (30:5).
views.H: "Uprisings" (neōterismoi) may point to the revolt at Corinth; Lake took the word as "youthful lusts."

echoes: Proverbs 3:34; James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5; Job 11:2–3; James 2:24; Hebrews 11:2; Colossians 3:12

settings.what: Against the man of many words (Job 11:2–3 in the Greek)
settings.by: Zophar the Naamathite, one of Job's friends (Job 11:1)
settings.to: Job; in the letter, the Corinthians
settings.why: To back the call to be "justified by works, not by words" (30:3) with Scripture against empty talk.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

title: The Paths of Blessing
sum: Clement unrolls the old story to find the paths of blessing. Abraham was blessed because he did righteousness and truth through faith (31:2). Isaac knew what was coming and was gladly led up to be sacrificed (31:3). Jacob, in humility, fled from his brother, served Laban, and received the scepter of the twelve tribes (31:4). Each received from God; none seized his blessing.

views.J: Clement makes Isaac a willing sacrifice who knew the outcome, as a Jewish retelling of the time does (4 Maccabees 13:12). Jacob's flight and service are told as humility, a theme the Genesis story leaves unspoken.
views.N: Abraham's faith and works stand together, as in Romans 4 and James 2; Isaac's confidence recalls Hebrews 11:17–19.

echoes: Genesis 15:6; Genesis 22:1–14; Genesis 27:41–28:5; Genesis 29:15–30; Romans 4:3; James 2:21–23; Hebrews 11:17–19; 4 Maccabees 13:12

settings.what: The patriarchs, and justification through faith
settings.by: The church of God in Rome, speaking as one body (tradition names Clement as the writer)
settings.to: The church of God at Corinth, "beloved," where a few members had led a revolt and removed elders who had served well (44:6; 47:6)
settings.why: To show from Israel's fathers that every blessing is God's gift, not a human achievement, and so to undercut the pride behind the revolt.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

title: Not Through Ourselves, but Through Faith
sum: Look closely, says Clement, and you will see how great God's gifts were. From Jacob came the priests and Levites, the Lord Jesus in his human descent, and the kings of Judah, and the other tribes were held in glory, as God promised offspring like the stars (32:1–2). All were glorified "not through themselves or their works ... but through his will" (32:3). So too Christians, called in Christ Jesus, are justified not through their own wisdom, understanding, godliness or holy works, but through faith, by which God Almighty has justified all from the beginning (32:4).
readings: Read with Paul

32:4 is close to Romans 3:28 and Ephesians 2:8–9: justification comes through faith, not through anything we do, even works "in holiness of heart." Lightfoot (1890) calls it an emphatic declaration "that men are not justified by their own works but by faith."
Read with 30:3 and 33:1

Clement has just said "justified by works, not by words" (30:3) and goes straight on to "every good work" (33:1). Lightfoot sees a "studied effort to keep the balance" between Paul and James, and ties it to Clement's place in a church of Jewish and Gentile Christians.

views.N: "In his human descent" (32:2) is the phrase of Romans 9:5; "not justified through ourselves ... but through faith" (32:4) recalls Romans 3:28, Ephesians 2:8–9 and Titus 3:5.
views.O: The churches' own answers on faith and works are on the site's cards at Romans 3, James 2 and Joshua 2.
views.H: Lake notes that the chapter division breaks Clement's thought: 32:1 belongs with 31:4, "by him" means God, and "from him" in 32:2 means Jacob.

deep.b:
Three sentences in four chapters set the terms. "Be justified by works, not by words" (30:3). "We ... are not justified through ourselves ... or through works we have done in holiness of heart, but through faith" (32:4). "Are we to sit idle, stop doing good, and leave love behind? May the Master never let that happen" (33:1).

32:4 is close to Paul's words: faith, not works of any kind, is how God justifies. 33:1 asks the question Paul asked in Romans 6:1, whether grace makes good works pointless; Lightfoot (1890) calls it "evidently modelled on Rom. vi. 1." 30:3 sets real deeds against mere talk, as James 2 does.

Lightfoot reads the three together. After "declaring emphatically that men are not justified by their own works but by faith," Clement "hastens to balance this statement by urging the importance of good works," as he joins faith and hospitality in Abraham (10:7) and Rahab (12:1). Lightfoot calls it a "studied effort to keep the balance," which "produces a certain incongruous effect in the rapid transition," and links it to Clement's position in a community where Jewish and Gentile Christians "had been in direct antagonism." Clement himself does not say how the sentences fit together.

The text itself shows two things clearly. Clement's main point in 31–32 is humility: no one, from Abraham to the Roman and Corinthian Christians, has glory "through themselves." And faith is never idle for him: the next chapter begins with God's own joy in work. How these fit into the later Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed and other accounts of justification is set out, with each church's own words, on the site's cards at Romans 3, James 2 and Joshua 2.

deep.title: Claude's theory: justification as a cure for faction
deep.b: Clement's teaching on faith comes inside an argument against pride (30:1–8; 39:1). The rebels at Corinth, he says elsewhere, acted in arrogance (14:1). If no one, not even Abraham, is justified "through themselves" or by "wisdom or understanding," then no faction can claim to be better than the elders it removed. I read 32:4 as doctrine put to pastoral use: justification by faith makes humility the only fitting posture. This is my own reading. Lightfoot (1890) makes a related point when he ties Clement's balance of Paul and James to his place as a reconciler.

echoes: Romans 3:28; Romans 4:2–5; Romans 9:4–5; Ephesians 2:8–10; Titus 3:5; James 2:14–26; Genesis 15:5; Genesis 22:17; Genesis 26:4

title: Do Not Stop Doing Good
sum: Does faith mean we may stop doing good? "May the Master never let that happen" (33:1). God himself rejoices in his works (33:2). He set the heavens in place, separated land from sea, made the animals, and shut in the sea by his power (33:3). Above all he shaped the human being with his own hands, the stamp of his own image, as Genesis 1:26–28 says (33:4–6). The righteous are adorned with good works, as the Lord himself was; with this model to trace before us, let us work the work of righteousness with all our strength (33:7–8).

views.N: The question of 33:1 is the shape of Romans 6:1. "The stamp of his image" uses Hebrews 1:3's word charaktēr.
views.J: Genesis 1:26–28 is quoted from the Septuagint, shortened; Clement's "he praised them" stands for Genesis 1:31's "very good."
views.G: The ordered creation of 33:3 continues the picture of chapter 20: a cosmos in harmony under its Maker.

echoes: Romans 6:1–2; Genesis 1:26–31; Genesis 2:7; Job 38:8–11; Psalm 104:5–9; Hebrews 1:3; Ephesians 2:10

settings.what: Good works after faith, from the Creator's example
settings.by: The church of God in Rome, speaking as one body (tradition names Clement as the writer)
settings.to: The church of God at Corinth, "beloved," where a few members had led a revolt and removed elders who had served well (44:6; 47:6)
settings.why: To block the conclusion that faith makes good works unnecessary, and to call the Corinthians to work together like the angels who serve God in harmony (34:5–7).
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

settings.what: God's words at creation (Genesis 1:26–28)
settings.by: God, as Genesis presents him
settings.to: In Genesis, the divine "us" and then the first humans; in the letter, the Corinthians
settings.why: To show that the God who made humankind in his image delighted in his works, and so his people should delight in good works too.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

title: The Good Worker and the Angels' Song
sum: The good worker takes his pay without shame; the lazy one cannot face his employer (34:1). So be eager to do good, for the Lord is coming with his reward to pay each by his work (34:2–4). Let our boast be in him, and let us submit to his will, like the countless angels who stand and serve him and cry "Holy, holy, holy" (34:5–6, joining Daniel 7:10 and Isaiah 6:3). So the gathered church, in harmony, should cry out to God "as if from one mouth" for a share in his promises (34:7), the things no eye has seen, prepared for those who wait for him (34:8).

views.N: 34:3 blends Isaiah 40:10, 62:11 and Proverbs 24:12 as Revelation 22:12 does; 34:8 is 1 Corinthians 2:9, ending with Isaiah 64:4's "those who wait for him."
views.J: Daniel 7:10 is given with the verb of Theodotion's Greek, and Isaiah 6:3 with "all creation" for "the earth." Jewish prayer also sets Isaiah 6:3 in worship (the site's Isaiah 6:3 note names the Kedushah).
views.O: The site's note on Isaiah 6:3 links 34:6–7 to the church's use of the "Holy, holy, holy" (the Sanctus) in the Eucharist, a use "already hinted at" here. The text calls for one voice in prayer; it does not describe the service.

deep.h: "Holy, holy, holy" in heaven and in the gathered church
deep.b:
Clement sets two pictures side by side: the angels who "stood beside him" and "served him" crying "Holy, holy, holy" (34:6), and the church "gathered together in one place in harmony" crying out "as if from one mouth" (34:7). The verb "served" (leitourgeō) is the root of "liturgy," and "in one place" (epi to auto) is the New Testament's phrase for the church assembled (Acts 2:1; 1 Corinthians 11:20). The site's note on Isaiah 6:3 says that Christians sing that verse in the Sanctus of the Eucharist, and that this use is already hinted at here.

Whether the Roman church already sang the seraphs' words in its worship is not stated. What Clement plainly asks for is unity: as the angels serve God together, each in his place (compare 37), so the church should pray with one heart. The theme ties his liturgy to his politics. Harmony in worship is the opposite of the split at Corinth.

echoes: Isaiah 6:3; Daniel 7:10; Revelation 4:8; Revelation 22:12; Isaiah 40:10; Isaiah 62:11; Proverbs 24:12; 1 Corinthians 2:9; Isaiah 64:4; Titus 3:1; Acts 2:1

settings.what: The heavenly court and the seraphs' cry (Daniel 7:10 and Isaiah 6:3, joined)
settings.by: The countless angels who serve God, as Daniel saw them in his dream (Daniel 7:1) and Isaiah in his vision "in the year King Uzziah died" (Isaiah 6:1)
settings.to: God; in the letter, the Corinthians, who are to join with one voice (34:7)
settings.why: To set the angels' ordered service before a divided church as the model for its own worship.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

settings.what: What God has prepared (1 Corinthians 2:9, ending with Isaiah 64:4)
settings.by: Scripture, as Paul quotes it ("as it is written," 1 Corinthians 2:9), with Isaiah's "those who wait for him"
settings.to: Paul's Corinthians first; now the same church again
settings.why: To promise the Corinthians a share in what God has prepared, if they wait for him with one heart.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

title: The Gifts of God, and the Sinner God Rebukes
sum: God's gifts are blessed and amazing: life in immortality, brightness in righteousness, truth, faith, self-control (35:1–2). What he prepares for those who wait only he knows; so we should strive to be among them (35:3–4). The way is to fix the mind on God, do his will, and throw off the sins Romans 1 lists, from unrighteousness to pride and inhospitality (35:5). Those who approve such things are as guilty as those who do them (35:6). Psalm 50 in Greek then gives God's rebuke to the sinner who recites his covenant but slanders his brother, and ends with the sacrifice of praise, the way to God's salvation (35:7–12).

views.N: 35:5–6 follows Romans 1:29–32 closely, ending with its last line. The "sacrifice of praise" (35:12) is the phrase of Hebrews 13:15.
views.J: Psalm 50:16–23 is quoted from the Septuagint (Psalm 49), with "like a lion" added at 35:11, which neither Swete nor Rahlfs prints.
views.H: The last word of the vice list is uncertain in the witnesses (see the variant): "inhospitality," "love of glory," or an impossible "hospitality."

settings.what: God's gifts, the way to them, and Christ the high priest
settings.by: The church of God in Rome, speaking as one body (tradition names Clement as the writer)
settings.to: The church of God at Corinth, "beloved," where a few members had led a revolt and removed elders who had served well (44:6; 47:6)
settings.when: after the call to good works (33–34)
settings.why: To set the promised gifts before a church tempted by slander and pride, and to show that the way to them is Jesus Christ.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

settings.what: God's rebuke to the sinner (Psalm 50:16–23)
settings.by: God, speaking in the psalm
settings.to: In the psalm, the one who recites God's covenant while living wickedly; in the letter, the Corinthians who slander their brothers
settings.why: To make the Corinthians hear God's own judgment on people who talk about his covenant and tear down their brothers.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

title: Jesus Christ, Our High Priest
sum: The way of salvation is Jesus Christ, "the high priest of our offerings, the protector and helper of our weakness" (36:1). Through him we look into heaven, see God's face as in a mirror, have the eyes of our heart opened, and taste immortal knowledge (36:2). In words taken from Hebrews 1, he is the brightness of God's majesty, greater than the angels (36:2). The angels are servants (36:3), but to the Son the Master said "You are my son" and "Sit at my right hand, until I set your enemies down as a footstool for your feet" (36:4–5). The enemies are those who oppose his will (36:6).

views.N: Clement follows Hebrews 1:3–13 closely: the same order of argument, the same psalms, and some of the same words. Clement does not name Hebrews. Lightfoot (1890) holds that "the whole passage is borrowed from the opening of the Epistle to the Hebrews."
views.H: Eusebius saw that Clement "gives many thoughts drawn from the Epistle to the Hebrews" and uses its words, and drew from this that Hebrews was not a recent writing (Church History 3.38.1–3).
views.O: "High priest of our offerings" is read in light of 40–44, where Clement speaks of offerings and of elders who presented the gifts. How the churches understand Christ's priesthood and the church's ministers is on the cards at Hebrews 7 and Hebrews 10.

deep.b:
Set side by side, 1 Clement 36 and Hebrews 1 run in the same order. Hebrews 1:3–4 calls the Son "the brightness that shines out from God's glory" and says he "became better than the angels" because of the name he inherited; Clement has "the brightness that shines out from God's majesty" and "greater than the angels by as much as the name he has inherited is more excellent." Then both quote Psalm 104:4 on the angels (Hebrews 1:7), Psalm 2:7 to the Son (Hebrews 1:5), and Psalm 110:1 (Hebrews 1:13). Clement adds Psalm 2:8, which Hebrews does not quote, and his own question, "Who, then, are the enemies?"

Which way did the borrowing go? Eusebius took the likeness as proof that Hebrews was older than 1 Clement, and reports that some thought Clement had put Paul's Hebrew letter into Greek, a view he himself favored because of the likeness of style (Church History 3.38.1–3). Lightfoot (1890) takes the same direction: "the whole passage is borrowed from the opening of the Epistle to the Hebrews, from which expressions, arguments, and quotations alike are taken." He notes that Clement gives Psalm 104:4 "exactly as in Heb. i. 7," with "a flame of fire" (pyros phloga), where the Septuagint manuscripts B and S have "burning fire" (pyr phlegon). The site's introduction to Hebrews uses Clement's echo to date Hebrews before about AD 96 and as one reason for placing it in Rome.

echoes: Hebrews 1:3–13; Hebrews 2:17–18; Hebrews 4:14–16; Psalm 104:4; Psalm 2:7–8; Psalm 110:1; 2 Corinthians 3:18; Ephesians 1:18

settings.what: God's words to the Son (Psalm 2:7–8; Psalm 110:1)
settings.by: "The Master," God the Father, as Clement and Hebrews read the psalms
settings.to: The Son
settings.when: quoted in the order Hebrews 1 uses
settings.why: To show that Christ, the church's high priest, rules over the angels and will see his enemies defeated, so that those who oppose God's will at Corinth stand on the wrong side.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

title: The Army and the Body
sum: Let us serve as soldiers under God's orders (37:1). Look at the soldiers who serve under our commanders: orderly, steady, obedient (37:2). Not all are prefects or officers over a thousand, a hundred or fifty, but each does in his own rank what the emperor and commanders order (37:3). The great need the small, and the small the great; there is a blending in all (37:4). So with the body: head and feet need each other, the smallest parts are necessary, and all "breathe together" in one submission to keep the whole body safe (37:5).
readings: Read as a lesson in order
Clement's point is rank: each soldier and each member has a place and a task. This prepares for 40–44, where he argues that God set an order of ministry in the church.
Read as a lesson in mutual need

The army and the body show not only rank but dependence: the great cannot exist without the small (37:4). Read this way, the passage asks the powerful as much as the lowly to keep their place in love.

views.G: Clement admires the Roman army from inside Rome ("our commanders"). The body picture was a famous Roman lesson in concord: Livy tells how Menenius Agrippa ended a strike of the common people with the fable of the members who rebelled against the belly (History of Rome 2.32).
views.N: The body is Paul's picture in 1 Corinthians 12:12–27, written to the same church; "blending" echoes 1 Corinthians 12:24.
views.J: The officers "of a thousand, of a hundred, of fifty" are the ranks Moses set over Israel (Exodus 18:21), not Roman titles.

deep.h: Army, body and the Roman ideal of concord
deep.b:
Clement uses two pictures his Roman and Greek hearers knew well. The army was the empire's great example of discipline, and Clement points to it directly: "our commanders" and "the emperor" (37:2–3). His ranks blend the Roman (prefects, tribunes, centurions) with the Greek Bible's "captains of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties and of tens" (Exodus 18:21).

The body was the classic picture of civic harmony. Livy tells that when the common people of Rome withdrew from the city, the senate sent Menenius Agrippa, because there was "no hope left, save in the concord of the citizens." He told them that the members once rebelled against the belly and starved, until they learned that the belly fed them all (History of Rome 2.32, Spillan's translation). Paul used the body for the church at Corinth (1 Corinthians 12), and Clement writes to that church again with both images in mind: a church in revolt is a body at war with itself.

echoes: 1 Corinthians 12:12–27; 1 Corinthians 15:23; Exodus 18:21; 2 Timothy 2:3–4; Ephesians 6:10–17; Romans 12:4–5

settings.what: The church as an army and a body
settings.by: The church of God in Rome, speaking as one body (tradition names Clement as the writer)
settings.to: The church of God at Corinth, "beloved," where a few members had led a revolt and removed elders who had served well (44:6; 47:6)
settings.when: after the high priesthood of Christ (36)
settings.why: To show that order and mutual service, not equality of rank, keep a body alive, and so to prepare the argument of 40–44 that the removed elders held a God-given place.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.

title: Each for the Other
sum: Let the whole body be kept safe in Christ Jesus, each submitting to his neighbor by the gift he has (38:1). The strong should care for the weak and the weak respect the strong; the rich should supply the poor, and the poor thank God for them; the wise should show wisdom in deeds; the humble should let others praise them; and the sexually pure should not boast, since God gives self-control (38:2). Remember where we came from, out of a "tomb and darkness" (the womb, or the earth we were made from), brought into God's world by his kindness (38:3). We owe him thanks for everything (38:4).

views.N: Gifts (charisma) and mutual care recall 1 Corinthians 12 and Romans 12; the rich and the poor recall 2 Corinthians 8–9; the strong and the weak, Romans 15:1.
views.O: 38:2's warning to the "pure in the flesh" is an early Christian word on celibacy; Ignatius of Antioch gives the same warning against boasting (Ignatius to Polycarp 5:2). How the churches regard celibacy is on the celibacy topic page.
views.H: Two readings of Codex Alexandrinus in 38:2 are damaged (see the variants).

echoes: 1 Corinthians 12:4–26; Romans 12:3–8; Romans 15:1; 2 Corinthians 8:13–15; 2 Corinthians 9:12; 1 Corinthians 4:7; Psalm 139:13–16

title: What Can a Mortal Do?
sum: Foolish, untaught people mock us and lift themselves up (39:1). But what can a mortal do, or a child of the earth (39:2)? Clement answers with Job 4:16–5:5 in Greek, the vision of Job's friend Eliphaz: no mortal is pure before the Lord, who finds fault even in his angels; people who live in houses of clay are crushed like a moth and die without wisdom (39:3–6). No holy angel will answer them; anger and jealousy kill the senseless; their home is eaten up and their sons are far from safety (39:7–9).

views.J: Clement quotes Eliphaz's words as "written" Scripture, from the Septuagint, which differs from the Hebrew in many lines, and adds a line from Job 15:15. At the end of Job, God says Eliphaz did not speak rightly about him (Job 42:7); Clement, like Paul in 1 Corinthians 3:19, uses the friends' words for truths they state well.
views.H: The mockers of 39:1 are unnamed. The words repeat 21:5; they may mean the leaders of the revolt (14:1), but the text does not say.
views.N: "Jealousy puts to death" (39:7) brings back Clement's opening theme (3–6) and James 3:16.

settings.what: Against the proud, with Eliphaz's vision (Job 4:16–5:5)
settings.by: The church of God in Rome, speaking as one body (tradition names Clement as the writer); inside it, Eliphaz the Temanite, quoted as Scripture
settings.to: The church of God at Corinth, "beloved," where a few members had led a revolt and removed elders who had served well (44:6; 47:6); inside the quotation, Job
settings.when: closing the first half of the letter, before the order of worship and ministry (40–44)
settings.why: To deflate the pride of those who mock the church's order, by reminding them that a mortal made of clay has no strength or purity of his own.
settings.readers: The Corinthian church, hearing the letter read aloud when the Roman messengers Claudius Ephebus, Valerius Bito and Fortunatus brought it (65:1). Lake dates it between 75 and 110, most likely the last decade of the first century.
